items.title: The angles of a triangle on a globe don't add to 180 degrees
items.claim: Draw a triangle from the North Pole to the equator at 0 degrees longitude, along the equator to 90 degrees longitude, and back to the North Pole. All three angles are 90 degrees. Total: 270.
items.prompt: How can a triangle have 270 degrees?

options.text: On a curved surface, the angle sum exceeds 180 by an amount proportional to the area enclosed (spherical excess); on a sphere of radius R, sum = 180 + (area / R^2) in radians times 180/pi

items.reveal:
On a flat Euclidean plane, the angles of a triangle sum to exactly 180 degrees.

On a sphere (positive curvature), the sum is more than 180. The excess is proportional to the area: Sum - 180 = (Area / R^2) * (180/pi) for a sphere of radius R. The example triangle (pole-equator-equator-pole) covers 1/8 of the Earth's surface — area ~ 6.4 * 10^7 square km — and has excess 90 degrees.

On a hyperbolic plane (negative curvature), the sum is LESS than 180. The deficit is proportional to area.

This is the deepest test of non-Euclidean geometry: by measuring the angle sum of a triangle, you can tell what kind of space you're in.

Gauss attempted to measure the angle sum of a triangle formed by three mountain peaks (Hohenhagen, Brocken, Inselsberg) in 1820s to test whether space itself is Euclidean. He found no measurable deviation from 180, given his instruments' precision.

General relativity: mass curves space-time. Light follows geodesics through curved space-time. Two photons from a distant source, passing on either side of the Sun, converge (negative curvature in tested region's measurement frame). Detected during the 1919 solar eclipse — confirmation of Einstein.
items.why: Triangles seem to obviously sum to 180. They do on flat surfaces. Real Earth navigation, general relativity, and modern cosmology all use non-Euclidean geometry where triangle sums are observably different.

items.title: London to Tokyo flights cross Siberia — not because Russia is convenient
items.claim: On a flat map, the shortest path between London and Tokyo looks like a horizontal line through Central Asia. The ACTUAL shortest path on Earth's surface arcs north over Siberia. That's the great-circle route.
items.prompt: Why is the great-circle route shortest?

options.text: Any geodesic (shortest path) on a sphere is part of a great circle — a circle whose plane passes through the sphere's centre. Latitude lines (except the equator) are NOT great circles, so flying along a latitude isn't optimal

items.reveal:
A geodesic is the shortest path between two points on a surface. On a flat plane, geodesics are straight lines. On a sphere, geodesics are arcs of great circles — circles whose centre coincides with the sphere's centre.

All meridians (longitude lines, including the prime meridian and date line) are great circles. The equator is a great circle. Lines of latitude EXCEPT the equator are NOT great circles — they're small circles whose plane does not pass through Earth's centre.

London-Tokyo: separated by ~9600 km along the great-circle route, ~12000 km if you fly along the line of latitude (~50°N).

Map projections distort geodesics:
- Mercator projection (Gerardus Mercator, 1569): preserves angles (conformal), shows rhumb lines as straight, but distorts areas and great-circle paths.
- Gnomonic projection: shows great circles as straight lines, but is unsuitable as a navigational chart.
- Robinson, Mollweide: balance distortions in different ways.

Airlines plan routes along great circles, adjusted for winds (jetstream eastbound from US to Europe saves an hour). 'Polar' routes from North America to East Asia routinely cross the Arctic.

In general relativity, geodesics on curved spacetime trace the paths of free-falling objects — gravity IS geodesic motion through curved spacetime.
items.why: Maps lie about distances. Modern navigation requires understanding that the shortest path on a sphere is curved on a flat map. The intuition fails everywhere except locally.

items.title: Tilting your phone changes things differently depending on the order
items.claim: Take a book. Rotate 90 degrees about its vertical axis, then 90 degrees about its horizontal axis. Now reset and reverse the order: horizontal first, then vertical. The book ends up in a DIFFERENT orientation. Rotations in 3D do not commute.

options.text: Rotation matrices in 3D are non-commutative — R1 * R2 is not equal to R2 * R1 in general. SO(3) is a non-abelian Lie group, unlike rotations in 2D which DO commute

items.reveal:
Rotations in 2D (the plane): R(theta1) * R(theta2) = R(theta1 + theta2) = R(theta2) * R(theta1). They commute. The group SO(2) is abelian.

Rotations in 3D: not commutative. The group SO(3) is non-abelian. The order in which you apply rotations changes the final orientation.

Experiment: rotate book 90° about vertical (y-axis) — left becomes back. Then rotate 90° about (now front-pointing) x-axis — back becomes bottom. Reset. Now rotate 90° about x first — top becomes back. Then 90° about y — back becomes left. Final orientations differ.

Mathematically: if R_x is rotation about x-axis and R_y about y-axis, R_x R_y is not equal to R_y R_x. The 'commutator' [R_x, R_y] = R_x R_y - R_y R_x is non-zero, representing a small rotation about the third axis.

Consequences:
- Aerospace: gimbal lock — a 3-axis gyroscope can have its three rotation axes align such that one rotational degree of freedom is lost. Famously almost killed Apollo astronauts on Apollo 11.
- Quaternions (Hamilton 1843) parametrise 3D rotations without gimbal lock and are standard in 3D graphics.
- Quantum mechanics: angular momentum operators have the same commutation structure as 3D rotations, leading to quantisation.

In higher dimensions (n > 3), rotation groups SO(n) are also non-commutative.
items.why: Rotation seems like a simple geometric concept. In 3D it's surprisingly subtle — the order matters, and that fact has cost lives, structured quantum mechanics, and shaped every video game engine.
